newsitem.title: UK: IBCA affirms Czech A minus foreign currency rating.
newsitem.headline: IBCA affirms Czech A minus foreign currency rating.

text.p: IBCA, the European credit rating agency, said on Monday it had confirmed its long-term foreign currency rating of A minus for the Czech Republic.
"The rating applies to senior and unsecured sovereign debt issues and sets a ceiling for all other Czech issuers," IBCA said in a statement.
"This solid investment grade rating is equalled among the group of post-communist countries only by Slovenia," IBCA said.

"It reflects the Czech Republic's exceptionally low level of public sector indebtedness, both domestic and external, its extremely modest debt service ratios, and its track record of sound macroeconomic management, all of which carry considerable weight in our assessment."
But the agency said the Republic's rating was constrained by the fact that its market economy was still very young.

"Market structures in the western sense are still weak, commercialisation of newly privatised enterprises is still at an early stage, the corporate sector as a whole is woefully under-capitalised, and there are legitimate concerns about the quality of corporate governance," IBCA said.
IBCA said there was an "evident and pressing" need for reforms at the microeconomic level.
"However, progress in this area could be delayed by the less self-assured macroeconomic and political climate currently prevailing," it added.
IBCA said a shift into trade deficit was to be expected in an economy moving out of prolonged recession and where restructuring must be accompanied by increased imports of capital goods.

"However, the size and speed of the deterioration in the Czech Republic's case would normally ring alarm bells, given its accompaniments of excessive wage increases, fast growing consumption, overfull employment, high monetary growth and renewed upwards pressure on inflation," IBCA said.
"We expect the current account deficit to exceed six percent of GDP this year -- in relative terms, the largest of all the east European countries in transition," the statement said.

"While the exceptional buildup in foreign exchange reserves in 1995 means there is no immediate cause for concern, this level of imbalance is unlikely to be sustainable into the longer term when it would undoubtedly foment speculative pressures against the currency," it said.
